title: TaxGPT vs Thomson Reuters Checkpoint
summary: Compare TaxGPT vs. Thomson Reuters Checkpoint: AI‑powered research with real‑time primary sources, faster answers, and 6× lower cost—upgrade your tax workflow.
body_markdown:
A founder I work with forwarded me a signed term sheet late on a Friday: a strategic buyer wanted her SaaS company, with the deal set to close in three weeks. Her question was the one every founder asks the moment a liquidity event becomes real: *how much of this do I actually keep?* Roughly $9 million of gain was on the table, all of it on stock she'd held in her C corporation since founding.


The answer turned on Section 1202, the qualified small business stock (QSBS) exclusion. Did her shares qualify? Had she cleared the five-year holding period, and was she inside the per-issuer cap? And with the 2025 tax law reshaping QSBS for newer stock, did any of the new rules change the math? This is exactly the kind of moment where the tool you reach for either buys you time or costs you an evening, and here it was the difference between a largely tax-free exit and a seven-figure capital-gains bill.


I spent years doing exactly this kind of work by hand: logging into a research library, running searches, opening editorial notes, cross-checking primary law, and assembling an answer piece by piece. It works. It's also slow, and slow is expensive when a client is waiting.


That experience is why I want to be precise in this comparison. Checkpoint, now with Checkpoint Edge and CoCounsel, has real generative AI, so this isn't "AI vs. no AI." The question that actually decides it is different: what kind of AI, and how much of your firm's work it can actually do. That's where the two products stop looking alike.


TaxGPT isn't a digital library you search through. It's an[AI-powered tax operating system](https://www.taxgpt.com/ai-operating-system) that unifies research, client intelligence, return review, return preparation, planning, and autonomous agentic workflows in one place, sitting on top of the software your firm already runs. Built by tax professionals, for tax professionals.

### Why This Matters Now


For a long time, Checkpoint was the gold standard: a deep, authoritative research library that set the bar for its era.


Then generative AI arrived, and the *format* of tax work started to change, from "search and read and interpret" to "ask and get a cited answer." Thomson Reuters responded with Checkpoint Edge and CoCounsel, a real generative-AI research assistant. But the shift underneath is bigger than research: firms increasingly want AI that doesn't just *answer* a question but *does the work* . It prepares the return, reviews it, remembers the client, and runs the workflow.


That's the axis this comparison lives on. Checkpoint (with CoCounsel) helps you research and analyze. TaxGPT is built to run the whole engagement. It's why more than 80,000 users now run on TaxGPT: the productivity gap became impossible to ignore.


That said, if research is genuinely the only piece of the workflow you're looking to upgrade, and your firm is already deep in the Thomson Reuters ecosystem, Checkpoint's research layer alone may still be the simpler near-term fit. The rest of this comparison is about what happens once a firm wants that same AI applied past research, into prep, review, and planning.


## AI Models: Why TaxGPT's Technology Wins


Let me be accurate about what each side actually ships.


Checkpoint Edge with CoCounsel is a generative-AI research assistant built for tax and accounting professionals. You can ask plain-language questions and get cited, hallucination-mitigated answers drawn from Thomson Reuters' vetted primary law plus 12M+ editorial resources. It has been generally available in the US since 2024. As a way to find and read the law faster, it works.


But that's where it stops, and where TaxGPT keeps going:


- A purpose-built tax model. TaxGPT runs a tax-specific model layer fine-tuned on tax scenarios and reviewed by CPAs and tax attorneys. It has also[been benchmarked against OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini models for accuracy and hallucination rates on tax research](https://www.taxgpt.com/blog/taxgpt-is-state-of-the-art-tax-llm) . When I say "state-of-the-art tax LLM," that's a benchmark you can read, not a slogan.
- Model-agnostic by design. TaxGPT isn't locked to one vendor's model. It routes to the best-performing frontier model for the task, on top of the proprietary tax layer.
- Breadth that does the work. CoCounsel automates research and analysis steps. TaxGPT extends the same intelligence into[preparation](https://www.taxgpt.com/ai-tax-preparation) ,[review](https://www.taxgpt.com/agent-andrew) ,[planning](https://www.taxgpt.com/ai-tax-planning) , and[autonomous workflows](https://www.taxgpt.com/cowork) .


Both have real GenAI. The difference is what it's pointed at: Checkpoint stays inside research, while TaxGPT's benchmarked, purpose-built model also prepares, reviews, plans, and runs the work across your firm.


## Speed: Seconds vs. Minutes


**With TaxGPT** : I ask the question in plain language. In about 10–15 seconds I get a structured, cited answer covering IRC § 1202, the five-year holding period and the per-issuer cap under § 1202(b), the C-corporation and active-business requirements, and the § 1045 rollover option for deferring gain that doesn't yet qualify. It even flags the 2025 changes to QSBS for stock acquired after July 4, 2025. From there I can draft a client memo laying out the after-tax outcome in under a minute with the writing assistant. Start to finish: a couple of minutes.


**With Checkpoint** : even with CoCounsel speeding up the research, pulling the primary law, checking the editorial commentary, and assembling a defensible, cite-checked answer for a question this specific still runs 15–30 minutes in our own side-by-side testing, once you account for interpretation and drafting. Your own time will vary with question complexity and how familiar you already are with the tool.


The gap isn't about who has AI. It's about how much of the *end-to-end task* the tool completes for you. TaxGPT takes you from question to drafted client memo; a research library takes you from question to raw material and leaves the rest on your desk.


[Try TaxGPT free →](https://www.taxgpt.com/demo)


## User Experience: Conversational Interface vs. Complex Navigation


I have very little patience for training manuals, and so do the people I work with. TaxGPT's interface is a conversation: ask, get cited answers, upload a document, keep going. There's voice chat and a mobile app for when I'm not at my desk.


Onboarding is genuinely fast. Most people are productive in their first session, and a short walkthrough of about 15 minutes is more than enough to get a new hire going.


Checkpoint's interface has modernized too, and its GenAI assistant lowers the old learning curve. The full research suite still rewards some ramp-up time if you want to use everything it offers. But the difference that actually matters isn't the chat box. Its scope: TaxGPT's single interface also covers prep, review, planning, and workflows, so there's one tool to learn instead of a research suite plus everything it can't do.


## Sources and Reliability: Primary Authority vs. Editorial Opinion


TaxGPT answers are grounded in primary sources (IRS Code, Treasury Regulations, and rulings) with citations attached so you can verify every claim. That matters most for client-facing work and IRS positions, where "the software said so" isn't an answer.


Checkpoint layers decades of editorial commentary over primary law, and CoCounsel surfaces cited answers from that corpus. That editorial layer can be handy, but it's still interpretation, and it moves on Thomson Reuters' update cycle. TaxGPT stays synced to the latest IRS guidance and always shows its primary sources, so what you cite is the law itself, current as of now.
